Prostate cancer: evading immunity, inspiring therapy
abstract: Prostate cancer (PCa) remains one of the most prevalent and lethal cancers in men, particularly in its metastatic form. Despite therapeutic advancements, resistance to therapy often leads to a castration-resistant state with genetic and molecular alterations that promote immune evasion and disease progression. Chronic inflammation and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) further exacerbate immune dysfunction. The suboptimal clinical success of current immunotherapies in advanced PCa underscores the urgent need to better understand the mechanisms underlying immune escape during disease progression and in response to therapeutic interventions. This review explores the key immune-evasive features of PCa, the contribution of the TME, and the immunotherapeutic strategies that have been clinically evaluated to improve outcomes in patients with advanced disease.

title: Precision targeting of stromal states in pancreatic cancer: a clinical perspective
abstract: Desmoplastic stroma defines pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), a highly lethal malignancy. This stroma drives tumor progression, immune evasion, drug resistance, and poor drug delivery. Although targeting tumor stroma has shown preclinical promise, most clinical trials have failed due to limited translational success. A major hurdle is the stroma's extreme heterogeneity and dynamic nature, meaning uniform treatments fail. Emerging evidence supports the existence of distinct 'stromal states' with differential biological functions and therapeutic vulnerabilities. Characterizing these states provides a framework to stratify patients and guide precise, stroma-directed therapies. This review summarizes the clinical landscape of PDAC stroma-targeting strategies, discusses distinct stromal states, and outlines emerging opportunities to exploit the stroma as a therapeutic axis in PDAC to improve clinical trial outcomes.

title: Drugging the undruggable: early phase trial shows trabectedin and low-dose irinotecan downregulate EWSR1::FLI1 and has clinical activity in advanced Ewing sarcoma
abstract: Targeting transcription factor fusion-positive cancers has proven challenging for decades. In SARC037, Grohar et al. show that histology-specific dosing of trabectedin and low-dose irinotecan is active in advanced Ewing sarcoma and downregulates EWSR1::FLI1 activity.

title: Cancer cell plasticity: new insights from developmental programs
abstract: Tumors represent a heterogeneous set of neoplastic diseases, each composed of an intricate network of cancer cells residing in multiple alternative phenotypic states. Transitions between these phenotypic states, often termed 'phenotypic plasticity', enable them to execute specific steps in tumor progression and to develop therapeutic resistance. The phenotypic plasticity of tumor cells is mediated, in part, by cellular processes that orchestrate normal embryonic development and are hijacked by tumors. In this review, we discuss the contributions of these developmental programs to cancer cell phenotypic plasticity. We focus on epithelial-mesenchymal transition and ciliogenesis programs and discuss new insights into the mechanistic roles of these cellular processes in cancer progression and response to treatment.

title: Accelerating rare cancer research: a Zebrafish-First Triage Strategy
abstract: Rare cancers collectively account for approximately a quarter of diagnosed cancers. However, these tumors remain understudied due to research constraints, including underfunding, scarce samples, and reliance on resource-intensive mouse models. We propose a Zebrafish-First Triage Strategy to screen potential therapeutic targets before mammalian validation and accelerate research and drug development.

title: RBM15 in leukemogenesis: an emerging regulator at the interface of RNA biology and hematopoiesis
abstract: RNA-binding motif protein 15 (RBM15) is a key regulator of hematopoiesis and leukemogenesis, linking RNA metabolism, epitranscriptomic regulation, and lineage specification. Identified through the RBM15::MKL1 fusion in acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AMKL), RBM15 functions within the N 6 -methyladenosine (m 6 A) writer complex, where its RNA-recognition motifs and Spen paralog and ortholog C-terminal domain enable site-specific methylation and protein recruitment. In hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, RBM15 supports stem cell quiescence, self-renewal, and balanced lineage output, with additional roles in B cell, myeloid, and megakaryocytic differentiation. Mechanistically, RBM15 links m 6 A deposition to chromatin regulation, RNA export, and splicing. This review summarizes RBM15 structure, function, and regulation and highlights its emerging roles in leukemia, including AMKL and myelodysplastic syndromes, while outlining key questions for future studies.

title: Host metabolism rewrites metastatic fate
abstract: Metastatic heterogeneity has traditionally been explained by tumor-intrinsic evolution. A recent study by Peng-Winkler et al. challenges this paradigm by demonstrating that hepatic steatosis instructs colorectal cancer liver metastasis through fatty acid-dependent myelocytomatosis oncogene protein (MYC) activation. These findings identify host metabolism as an independent determinant of metastatic fate and suggest that precision oncology should extend beyond tumor genomics.

title: Exploiting DNA damage tolerance for precision oncology
abstract: Unresolved DNA lesions trigger replication stress, forcing cancer cells to hijack DNA damage tolerance (DDT) networks, specifically translesion synthesis (TLS) and template switching, to sustain replication. While DDT prevents lethal fork collapse, error-prone TLS drives mutagenesis, tumor evolution, chemoresistance and radioresistance. Proliferating cell nuclear antigen post-translational modifications dynamically govern pathway selection. Cancer cells exploit this plasticity, creating actionable vulnerabilities such as postreplicative single-stranded DNA gaps. Emerging inhibitors targeting TLS polymerases, upstream regulators such as ubiquitin-specific peptidase 1 (USP1), and critical protein-protein interactions offer unprecedented opportunities for precision oncology. By integrating DDT inhibition with biomarkers such as homologous recombination deficiency and tumor mutational burden, we can drive synthetic lethality, sensitize tumors to genotoxic agents, suppress treatment-induced mutagenesis, and potentially enhance responses to immunotherapy.

title: Cancer-associated synonymous mutations target mRNA structures and protein activity
abstract: The role of adaptive mRNA structures in regulating gene expression in mammalian cells remains poorly understood. Synonymous mutations have been linked to a range of diseases, including cancer, yet their impact on cell biology remains largely unexplored. This opinion focuses on how cancer-associated synonymous mutations (CASMs) in the TP53 mRNA disrupt signal-induced mRNA structures and alter the activity of the encoded protein. CASM203 induces conformational changes that recapitulate those driven by PERK during the unfolded protein response, promoting expression of the p53/p47 isoform. By contrast, CASM22 and CASM34 interfere with DNA damage-induced RNA structures and affect full-length p53 activity. Together, these examples illustrate an underappreciated regulatory axis in which dynamic mRNA structures interface between upstream signalling pathways and downstream effector functions, with direct implications for tumour biology.

Heterotypic tumor microenvironments mirror dynamic wound-healing process
abstract: Tumors co-opt normal wound-healing programs to shape their immune microenvironment, yet how distinct immune states arise and influence therapy remains unclear. Here, we synthesize emerging evidence that tumors become locked in either proinflammatory or pro-resolution phases, defined by neutrophil- or macrophage-dominated ecosystems. These states not only remodel local tissues but also systemically reprogram hematopoiesis, creating self-reinforcing immune circuits that drive progression, metastasis, and treatment resistance. We highlight recent advances linking epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity, lipid metabolism, and myeloid dynamics into an integrated 'wound-healing clock' model. This framework provides a conceptual basis for patient stratification and suggests that therapeutically redirecting immune states may unlock new strategies to overcome resistance across cancer types.

title: Fusion-product control in hematologic cancers
abstract: Oncogenic fusions both drive hematologic cancers and enable precise measurable residual disease tracking, yet whether residual fusion products can be therapeutically controlled remains incompletely defined. Emerging genomic, RNA, and proteostasis strategies now frame fusion control as a layer-matched therapeutic strategy.

title: From fixed antibody–drug conjugates to programmable therapeutics
abstract: Antibody-drug conjugates have long been designed as fixed therapeutic entities. In Nature, Simó et al. introduce in vivo molecular assembly as an alternative strategy, prompting a broader question: could future cancer therapeutics be engineered by programming molecular interactions within patients rather than constructing increasingly complex drugs beforehand?

title: Lkb1 loss links dietary lipids to cancer cachexia
abstract: Cancer cachexia involves more than a caloric deficit. A recent study by Cross et al. in Science shows that dietary lipid composition exacerbates cachexia in LKB1/STK11-deficient lung cancer through local prostaglandin E 2 production and pulmonary sensory neuron activation. By linking local lipid metabolism to anorexia and wasting, these findings support precision nutritional interventions for cancer cachexia.

title: Not ‘cold’ but conditional: emerging principles of immunotherapy in colorectal cancer
abstract: Repeated Phase 3 failures have framed proficient mismatch repair/microsatellite stable colorectal cancer as 'cold' and immunotherapy-resistant. We argue that this resistance is conditional, shaped by disease stage, metastatic anatomy, spatial immune architecture, and therapeutic mechanism. Recognizing these principles can guide patient selection, biomarker stratification, and drug development to realize immunotherapy's clinical potential.

title: Next-generation tumor-agnostic targets on the horizon
abstract: Tumor-agnostic drug development reframes oncology around shared molecular dependencies rather than tissue origin, enabling efficient development for rare, actionable drivers across tumors. Since the first tumor-agnostic approval in 2017 for immunotherapy in microsatellite instability-high or mismatch repair-deficient tumors, the regulatory paradigm has expanded to high tumor mutation burden (TMB-H) cancers, oncogene-directed kinase inhibitors, such as NTRK, rearranged during transfection (RET), BRAF valine-to-glutamic acid substitution at codon 600 (BRAF V600E), and antibody-drug conjugate targeting Her2 overexpression, establishing proof of principle across modalities. In this review, we examine current tumor-agnostic approvals and emerging targets with pan-cancer potential: Kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene homolog (KRAS) variants [glycine-to-cysteine substitution at codon 12 (G12C), glycine-to-aspartic acid substitution at codon 12 (G12D), and active GTP-bound RAS (RAS(ON)) inhibitors; degraders; and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T)], methylthioadenosine phosphorylase (MTAP) loss (methylthioadenosine (MTA)-cooperative protein arginine methyltransferase 5 (PRMT5) and methionine adenosyltransferase 2A (MAT2A) inhibition), tumor protein p53 (TP53) tyrosine-to-cysteine substitution at codon 220 (Y220C) allele-specific reactivation, and fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 (FGFR2) and neuregulin (NRG) fusions. We explore critical challenges including standardized assays, endpoints, infrastructure, and access limitations. Finally, we outline features shaping next-generation programs: novel basket-trial designs, real-world evidence integration, and international collaborative frameworks. With molecules, infrastructure, and trial designs advancing in parallel, tumor-agnostic strategies are poised to deliver equitable benefit across cancers, realizing precision medicine without borders.

title: Macrophage-directed therapeutic strategies in cancer
abstract: Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) are a major component of the tumor microenvironment and exhibit remarkable functional plasticity, acting as either immunosuppressive cells that promote tumor progression or immunostimulatory cells that can support antitumor immunity, depending on the prevailing microenvironmental cues. These cells promote angiogenesis, metastasis, immune suppression, and therapy resistance. However, when appropriately reprogrammed, TAMs can directly kill or phagocytose cancer cells and/or activate antitumor T cell and natural killer cell responses. In this article, we review current therapeutic strategies targeting TAMs, including approaches directed against macrophage-associated receptors, signaling pathways, and epigenetic and metabolic regulators. We also discuss emerging TAM-targeted therapeutic modalities, including cytokine-based therapies, cell-based therapies, bispecific antibodies, macrophage-targeted nanoplatforms, and anti-TAM chimeric antigen receptor T-cell approaches, highlighting their potential to enhance antitumor immunity and improve clinical outcomes.

title: Integrating biology and mathematics to understand checkpoint immunotherapy
abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) elicit durable antitumor responses in immunogenic tumors but still fail in most patients. Extensive research has elucidated how ICIs trigger a wide array of antitumor responses, yet, unexpectedly, also fuel tumor immunosuppression, a major driver of therapy failure. We argue that the sheer number of variables at play will hinder upcoming research to improve ICI performance, making the classic experimental approach exceedingly time- and resource-intensive. We posit that this problem can be solved through a bidirectional feedback loop of mathematical modeling and experimental validation. This review consolidates foundational knowledge in cancer immunology and mathematical modeling and proposes strategies that enable mathematicians and immunologists to collaborate fruitfully and expedite breakthroughs in ICI therapy.

title: Circulating tumor cell–immune cell clusters: dynamic engines of metastasis
abstract: Circulating tumor cell (CTC) clusters are potent drivers of metastasis, exhibiting markedly greater metastatic capacity than single CTCs. Beyond homotypic CTC clusters, CTCs dynamically engage immune cells to form heterotypic clusters with enhanced metastatic fitness. Rather than passive assemblies, these clusters function as coordinated metastatic ecosystems, integrating adhesion, immune modulation, and metabolic adaptation to promote survival, plasticity, and immune evasion. Recent advances in CTC isolation, single-cell and spatial multiomics, and artificial intelligence-driven analyses have enabled unprecedented resolution of these dynamic interactions. Together, these findings support a conceptual shift from isolated single-cell dissemination to multicellular cooperation as an important principle of metastasis and identify CTC-immune cell clusters as actionable targets for next-generation therapies to boost immunity and prevent metastasis.

title: Precision before incision: neoadjuvant tumor-agnostic therapies
abstract: The emergence of tumor-agnostic therapies has fundamentally transformed precision oncology. Traditionally developed and approved for metastatic disease, nine therapies spanning immunotherapy, targeted agents, and antibody-drug conjugates now demonstrate a compelling rationale for earlier deployment in the neoadjuvant setting. This review examines the paradigm shift from last-resort to first-consideration approaches. Key advantages of neoadjuvant, biomarker-guided therapy include intervention prior to the development of therapeutic resistance, optimal immune system engagement, and opportunities for organ preservation. Single-agent programmed cell death protein-1 blockade has achieved a 100% complete response rate in mismatch repair-deficient rectal cancer with preserved organ function. Neurotrophic tyrosine receptor kinase (NTRK), rearranged during transfection (RET), and B-Raf proto-oncogene serine/threonine kinase (BRAF) inhibitors have demonstrated substantial responses that enable curative-intent surgery across malignancies. As precision oncology matures, the neoadjuvant tumor-agnostic approach exemplifies optimized therapeutic sequencing, potentially improving patient outcomes and quality of life.

title: Protecting axonal mitochondria prevents chemotherapy-driven neuropathy
abstract: Peripheral neuropathy is a poorly understood yet extraordinarily relevant obstacle to the effective implementation of cytotoxic chemotherapy in patients with cancer. Recent findings from Heles et al. demonstrate that safe neuroactive molecules that promote mitochondrial fitness in axons effectively prevent peripheral neuropathy in preclinical tumor models, thereby supporting clinical translation.

title: Enhancer of zeste homolog 2 links epigenetic plasticity to cholesterol metabolism
abstract: Enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2) is the catalytic subunit of Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), which mediates transcriptional repression. Kim and colleagues uncover a PRC2-independent EZH2-sterol regulatory element-binding protein 2 (SREBP2) axis that drives cholesterol biosynthesis, revealing an epigenetic-metabolic vulnerability exploitable through targeted protein degradation.

Emerging landscape of antibody–drug conjugates in lung cancer: a clinical review
abstract: Lung cancer is a heterogeneous disease, and while targeted therapies and immunotherapies have improved patient outcomes, 5-year overall survival remains poor at approximately 20%. Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) target tumors using a targeted antibody that delivers a cytotoxic payload with clinically proven antitumor activity, and over a dozen ADCs are under consideration for solid tumors. Recent clinical trial data in metastatic non-small cell lung cancer have led to FDA approval of three ADCs: trastuzumab deruxtecan for patients with human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-mutated disease, telisotuzumab vedotin for MET-overexpressing tumors, and datopotamab deruxtecan for patients with epidermal growth factor receptor-mutated disease. In this article, we review the trajectory of individual ADC targets in lung cancer, describe the latest clinical trial results, and discuss future innovations in ADC therapies and potential mechanisms of resistance.

title: MAIT cells in gastrointestinal cancer: immunity to therapy
abstract: Mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells are emerging as important regulators of immunity in gastrointestinal (GI) cancers. Enriched in mucosal and hepatic tissues, MAIT cells recognize microbial-derived metabolites presented by MHC class I-related molecule (MR1) and rapidly exert effector functions, including cytokine production and cytotoxicity. Across GI malignancies, including hepatocellular carcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, colorectal, gastric, pancreatic, and esophageal cancers, MAIT cells display context-dependent roles shaped by the tumor microenvironment, microbiome, and immune signaling pathways. While they can mediate antitumor immunity, they frequently exhibit functional exhaustion or adopt pro-tumorigenic phenotypes. Therapeutic strategies aim to enhance MAIT cell activity, reverse dysfunction, and integrate them into combinatorial immunotherapy approaches. Understanding MAIT cell biology may enable their exploitation as biomarkers and therapeutic targets in GI cancers.

title: The tumor macroenvironment as cancer metabolism’s next frontier
abstract: The deregulated utilization of nutrients by tumors, first observed over a century ago, is recognized as a hallmark of cancer and continues to be exploited clinically to image neoplastic disease. Despite this historic focus on cancer cells and, more recently, their neighbors, metabolic reprogramming is not limited to the tumor microenvironment. Tumors also have the capacity to rewire the metabolism of cells throughout the body, including those at distant sites, often referred to as the tumor macroenvironment. Alterations in the metabolism of noncancerous tissues outside the local tumor ecosystem are gaining attention, but their origins and consequences remain incompletely defined. A deeper understanding of these changes may reveal previously unrecognized signatures of disease and unexplored opportunities for therapeutic intervention.

title: Bispecific antibodies in NSCLC: immune reengineering to neutralize adaptive tumor resistance
abstract: Over the past few decades, the emergence of immunotherapy and single-target drugs has brought new promise to the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Yet the high heterogeneity of NSCLC leads to both primary and acquired resistance that neither sequential monotherapy nor empirical combinations can effectively overcome. In contrast to the conventional coadministration of two separate monoclonal antibodies, bispecific antibodies (BsAbs) feature a series of molecular engineering designs that confer inherent synergistic antitumor effects. We propose that a network pharmacology perspective can be adopted to understand the application of BsAbs in NSCLC and to guide their subsequent development.

title: Advancing functional treatment prediction for precision oncology
abstract: Personalized cancer treatment requires stratification of patients based on biomarkers. Despite advances in biomarker-guided therapy, biomarkers are not always available or sufficient to predict treatment responses in individual patients. Functional ex vivo cancer models with the potential to assess therapeutic outcomes upfront have been developed but have not been implemented in clinical practice-despite accumulating evidence of their clinical relevance. This review describes how three essential steps in the development of personalized functional prediction tests (analytical validity, clinical validity, and clinical utility) should be combined in a multidisciplinary approach: Integrated Translational Co-design. This approach front-loads clinical utility and validation constraints into early analytical design decisions, so that biological fidelity, clinical implementation, and healthcare costs can be optimized from the start of assay development.

title: Genome-wide human T cell screens: barriers and design
abstract: Liu et al. enabled genome-wide clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) screening of primary human T cells in vivo and identified P2RY8 and GNAS through complementary functional readouts. We discuss how context shapes perturbation effects, and how readouts guide prioritization, with implications for T cell engineering in solid tumors.

title: Accelerated aging and early-onset colorectal cancer
abstract: The rising incidence of early-onset colorectal cancer (EOCRC) challenges existing paradigms of tumorigenesis. Classical models based on cumulative mutational burden, environmental exposure, and hereditary predisposition fail to explain the emergence of malignancy in individuals under 50 years of age. In this review, we propose that EOCRC may be driven by accelerated biological aging and review how core aging processes are prematurely activated in EOCRC. Importantly, these alterations extend beyond the tumor microenvironment and are present in circulating immune cells and inflammatory mediators. We propose that EOCRC develops prematurely in response to environmental, metabolic, genetic, and related factors that systemically accelerate biological aging. This approach reconciles the origin of EOCRC with traditional models of tumorigenesis, while highlighting novel opportunities for early detection, risk stratification, and therapeutic intervention.

title: Exercise against cancer: recent advances and open questions
abstract: More than a century after observations linking muscular activity to reduced cancer risk, exercise oncology has progressed from epidemiological association to interventional evidence. Large cohort studies associate physical activity with reduced cancer incidence and mortality, and a Phase 3 randomized trial now demonstrates cancer-specific survival benefits of structured exercise. In parallel, preclinical and emerging human studies provide mechanistic insight into how exercise may modulate tumor biology, including effects on immune surveillance, vascular function, metabolism, and systemic signaling. Despite these advances, gaps remain-notably, the limited integration of exercise variables into oncology trials and sparse mechanistic data from patients, particularly in pediatric cancers. This opinion article synthesizes recent clinical and mechanistic advances and outlines priorities for biologically informed integration of exercise into cancer research and the standard of care.

title: Trends at 50: a mission that matters
A roadmap for quantifying metabolism in patients with cancer
abstract: Advancements in in vivo stable isotope tracing have revolutionized our understanding of cancer metabolism, transitioning the field from static metabolomic snapshots to dynamic metabolic pathway activities. However, interpreting raw fractional enrichment data presents significant biological and analytical challenges. This review systematically examines the methodological landscape of in vivo tracing, addressing the interpretive gap created by clinical constraints, such as single-timepoint surgical sampling. We dissect how secondary circulating tracers and the inherent heterogeneity of the tumor microenvironment can confound metabolic signals. We highlight the critical transition to metabolic flux analysis as the requisite computational step to overcome these challenges and to identify targetable metabolic vulnerabilities in precision oncology.

title: Navigating clinical decisions through cancer cartography
abstract: Multiplexed spatial profiling has shown that tumor architecture influences therapy response, yet few spatial phenotypes are in clinical use. We opine that the immediate priority is simplification and validation of complex spatial features. We draw a parallel to cartography: maps are useful because they carry a limited set of named features whose meaning is agreed. Tumor maps could be built the same way: from the presence of a defined cell type, its proximity to another, its location within a tissue compartment, its state of activation, or combinations of these. Such features may have more clinical applicability than variable, unsupervised two-dimensional 'neighborhoods'. We propose cancer cartography as the process of assembling such validated features into tumor maps that guide treatment selection.

title: Acral melanoma: a unique subtype requiring unique solutions
